subject: Praxis Health — options for private connectivity (VPC peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN)
messages:

Subject: Connecting Redwood Private — recommended path for Praxis

Hi Jasmine,

Thanks again for the demo last week. Praxis is moving toward a private deployment for our PHI workloads and the infra team asked me for a recommendation between three options: VPC peering (account-to-account), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints / NLB), or a site-to-site VPN into our on-prem data center. Their priorities are:

- End-to-end encryption and no internet egress for inference traffic
- Low single-digit ms latency from our app tier (us-west-2) to the model endpoints
- Simpler operational model (fewer cross-account networking objects)
- Auditability / minimal blast radius for compromised creds

We host most of our services in an on-prem colo but are running a big portion in us-west-2 in the Praxis AWS account. Can you outline the tradeoffs briefly and any constraints we should be aware of? Also: any preferences from Redwood on which pattern makes upgrades/rollouts easiest?

Appreciate it — Evan

--
Evan Brooks
VP, Platform Engineering | Praxis Health
From: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com>

Evan — thanks for the clear list of priorities. Short answer up front: we generally recommend a hybrid approach for customers with both on-prem and cloud footprints. Below is a short matrix, followed by a recommendation tailored to your requirements. I attached a one‑pager and an initial diagram.

Quick matrix (latency / security / ops / cross-account):
- VPC peering: lowest latency for same-region VPCs, simple L3 routing; no transitive peering (per‑account setup required); cross-account peering is supported but each peering is an object to manage. Good for high-throughput low-latency within AWS.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): strong security (private endpoints per service), no route-table peering changes, supports cross-account without exposing VPC routes; slightly higher per‑request cost and additional NLB overhead. Great for minimizing blast radius and removing broad network access.
- Site-to-site VPN: flexible for on‑prem -> cloud; depends on customer gateway throughput and encryption settings; can add latency and jitter vs native cloud paths.

Tailored recommendation for Praxis:
1) Use PrivateLink for Redwood control & inference control-plane traffic (API calls, auth, model selection). PrivateLink minimizes wide VPC exposure and fits your audit/no-egress requirement.
2) For heavy bulk payloads (if you need to stream large batches of requests or upload datasets from on‑prem), colocate an ingress VPC in your Praxis AWS account and use VPC peering to avoid extra hop costs and provide lower latency between app tier and the ingress VPC.
3) Keep a redundant S2S VPN from your colo to the Praxis AWS account for fallback and maintenance windows (also useful for initial bootstrap if you don't want to open BGP immediately).

Operational notes:
- We'll recommend PrivateLink endpoints per AZ and an NLB in our service account; Praxis will need to create interface endpoints in your VPCs.
- DNS: use private hosted zones and conditional forwarding so service names resolve to iface endpoints.
- For model rollouts, PrivateLink helps with safe fallbacks since traffic is scoped to the endpoint — we can rotate backends without broad route changes.

Next step: I want Ben from Solutions to add specifics on throughput and MTU considerations; Kim will confirm security/KMS checklist. Can we schedule a 30-min call? I included two attachments: praxis-reqs-summary.pdf and praxis-initial-options-diagram.png.

Thanks,
Jasmine Liu

On Wed, Nov 18, 2026 at 11:05 AM Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com> wrote:
> Evan — thanks for the clear list of priorities. Short answer up front: we generally recommend a hybrid approach...

Adding some technical trade-offs and practical numbers from an infra perspective:

PrivateLink (recommended control plane):
- Throughput: Interface endpoints accept traffic to NLBs — expect per‑AZ throughput constraints based on the NLB sizing; for steady high-TPS workloads we size a couple of NLB targets and tune connection reuse.
- Latency: adds ~1–3ms vs in‑VPC when using iface endpoints in the same AZ. Typically fine for sub‑10ms targets.
- Security: traffic never traverses the public internet; IAM + endpoint policies can lock down callers.

VPC peering (intra-AWS, low latency):
- Pros: L3 routing, no NAT for egress, bidirectional connectivity once peered.
- Cons: No transitive peering (if you want many AWS accounts to reach the Redwood endpoint you need multiple peerings OR an aggregated transit VPC). Peering also requires route table management and care with IP CIDR overlaps.

Site-to-site VPN (on-prem):
- Throughput depends on your customer gateway and AWS VGW/transit throughput. Expect higher jitter; for low-latency interactive inference this is often slightly worse than cross‑AZ AWS paths.
- Recommendation: use S2S for management/fallback and for bulk sync if you have large dataset uploads from colo.

Hybrid pattern we recommend for Praxis:
- PrivateLink for API/control + short inference bursts (keeps blast radius small).
- A peered ingress VPC in Praxis account for sustained/high-throughput local traffic (apps talk to that VPC; peering gives minimal latency).
- S2S VPN to colo as backup and for cost-effective archive uploads.

Operational checklist (short):
- Verify non-overlapping CIDRs for peering; if overlap exists, use PrivateLink or a transit model.
- Set MTU to 9001 only if the whole path supports jumbo frames; otherwise 1500.
- Use BFD for rapid route failover on S2S if you run BGP.
- Monitor TCP connection reuse and tune keepalive on client SDKs to reduce NLB connection churn.

I attached a short notes file (ben-private-deploy-notes.md) with rough throughput numbers and an example NLB target group sizing formula. Happy to walk through on the call.

—Ben
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Quick security items to add to the design:
- KMS / key separation: Praxis should use a customer-managed CMK (AWS KMS) and optionally an HSM for any key material that must never leave your control. We support envelope encryption so customer keys remain primary for access control.
- Audit logs: ensure VPC flow logs and PrivateLink Flow logs are enabled and forwarded to your SIEM (we recommend a dedicated ingest S3 + Glue partitioning to keep retention manageable).
- DNS hygiene: use private hosted zones and enforce DNS over TLS in your VPCs where available; avoid split‑brain by clearly documenting which zone names map to the interface endpoints.
- Egress controls: if you need absolute guarantee of zero internet egress for inference data, prefer PrivateLink + endpoint policies + VPC endpoint route table restrictions. Avoid public NAT egress.

I've put a brief checklist in kims-security-checklist.xlsx attached. Also, we will need Praxis' SOC2 questionnaire answers on data residency and access controls before we sign the Private deployment contract.

Kimberly Park
Security & Compliance, Redwood Inference
